summary: Add and subtract mixed numbers with like denominators (ages 9–10). Two routes are worth teaching: (a) operate on whole-number and fraction parts separately, which exposes the two signature difficulties — in addition the fraction parts can sum past a whole (2 3/5 + 1 4/5 → 3 + 7/5, regroup to 4 2/5), and in subtraction the first fraction can be smaller than the second, forcing a borrow (4 2/6 − 1 5/6: regroup 4 into 3 + 6/6); and (b) convert both to improper fractions, which sidesteps the borrow and is worth teaching as the cleaner fallback. Let the awkward subtraction motivate the improper method, keep the denominator a fixed unit throughout, and always tidy an improper fraction part back into a proper mixed number.
misconceptions: Adds across the fraction parts (3/5 + 4/5 → 7/10), applying whole-number addition to numerator and denominator
Subtracts smaller-from-larger in each column and never borrows (4 2/6 − 1 5/6 → 3 3/6, taking |2−5|=3)
Leaves an improper fraction part in the answer (3 7/5) instead of regrouping to 4 2/5
Miscounts when converting mixed to improper (2 3/5 → 10/5 then forgets the +3/5, or writes 5/5)

activities.title: Trade a whole for unit fractions: make the borrow and carry physical
steps: Work the subtraction 4 2/6 − 1 5/6 using whole tiles and fraction tiles that are locked to sixths so you cannot change the denominator.
Try to take away 5 sixths when you only have 2 — notice you are stuck. Break one whole tile into 6 sixths (the borrow), so you now have 8 sixths, and finish: 8/6 − 5/6 = 3/6, leaving 2 3/6 = 2 1/2.
Work the addition 2 3/5 + 1 4/5 the same way: gather the fifths, and when 5 fifths collect, fuse them into a fresh whole tile, giving 4 2/5.

Optionally model the same two problems on a number line: jump the whole numbers first, then the fraction parts, and watch a jump cross a whole boundary — the same regroup seen as a different representation.
Write each exchange as a number sentence: 4 = 3 + 6/6, and 7/5 = 1 + 2/5.
Say aloud whether the carry and the borrow are the same exchange running in opposite directions.
activities.insight: Borrowing is not a mysterious digit-move: it is literally trading one whole for its equivalent in the common unit fraction (1 = 6/6), and carrying is the reverse — fusing a whole-worth of unit fractions back into one whole. The denominator stays fixed because fifths only join with fifths.

activities.title: The improper-fraction fallback, side by side
steps: Rewrite 4 2/6 and 1 5/6 as improper fractions (26/6 and 11/6), subtract to get 15/6, then convert back: 15/6 = 2 3/6 = 2 1/2.
Do the same subtraction by the separate-parts borrow method and check both answers match.
When converting 2 3/5 to improper, count carefully: 2 wholes is 10/5, plus 3/5 is 13/5 — do not drop the +3/5 or stop at 5/5.
Decide which method you found cleaner for the subtraction, and explain why converting to improper removed the borrow.
activities.insight: Converting to improper fractions avoids the borrow entirely, so it is a reliable fallback when the subtraction needs regrouping; both methods give the same answer when done carefully.

activities.title: Estimate first to police the answer
steps: Before computing 2 3/5 + 1 4/5, estimate using the whole numbers: the sum is between 3 and 5, and since both fraction parts are large, near 4 1/2.
Compute the exact answer and check it sits close to your estimate.

Repeat for 4 2/6 − 1 5/6: whole-number subtraction gives about 3, but because 2/6 is less than 5/6 the fraction part pulls the answer down by about a half, so expect a result between 2 and 3, around 2 1/2 — then confirm 2 1/2 is reasonable.
For each result, ask: is the fraction part proper (numerator less than denominator)? If not, regroup.
activities.insight: An estimate that starts with the whole numbers and then adjusts for the fraction parts catches value errors such as a missed borrow (3 3/6 instead of about 2 1/2) or added denominators (3 7/10 instead of about 4 1/2), because a wrong answer no longer sits near the estimate. An un-regrouped answer like 3 7/5 has the correct value (it equals 4 2/5), so an estimate cannot catch it; the separate proper-fraction check does that job.

activities.title: Study a worked carry and a worked borrow
steps: Read a worked addition showing 2 3/5 + 1 4/5 with the step 7/5 revealed as 1 + 2/5, and explain in your own words why the whole-number part becomes 4.
Read a worked subtraction showing 4 rewritten as 3 + 6/6, and answer: why change the 4 into 3 and 6 more sixths?
Match each mixed number to its improper form (e.g. 4 2/6 ↔ 26/6).
activities.insight: Reading and explaining the regroup steps consolidates the meaning behind the exchange, even without acting it out yourself.

checkQuestion: Work these out, showing every step: first 2 3/5 + 1 4/5, then 4 2/6 − 1 5/6.
